events.text: They come up from the valley the way water comes down: slowly, then all at once. First one farmer with a complaint, then the whole quarrel behind him, nine people and a boundary stone carried on a litter like a sick grandmother. Somebody moved it in the night. Each household swears the other did. They set the stone down at the edge of your spring and look at you, and nobody is quite brave enough to speak first.

choices.text: Walk round the stone and the nine of them, slowly, head low

ok.log: Nine faces, nine smells. One of them smells of fresh earth under the nails and very old fear. You stop in front of him and lower your head, gently, and he sits down in the spring. The stone goes back where it came from by nightfall.

fail.log: Nine faces and the horn says nothing. You lie down and look at the stone instead. After an hour the two households are so embarrassed they settle it themselves, splitting the strip of field in half. It is not justice. It is not nothing.

choices.text: Lower your head at the man who swears the loudest (the horn: a lie)

effects.log: He swears by his ancestors, his rice and his eyesight, and every oath goes into your horn like a sliver of ice. You lower your head at him. He stops swearing. The stone goes home, and the valley learns the way to your spring.

choices.text: Go up the hill. Human quarrels are humans' business

effects.log: You go up into the birches and leave them with their stone. They carry it home again, still quarrelling. The next week they are back, with two more households.

events.text: The headman, {npc}, a lean old farmer with a wispy beard and a voice used to shouting across paddies, has had an idea. The whole village has built it in three days: a straw shelter on four posts in the corner of {his} yard, a bed of clean rice straw, a stone trough that somebody scrubbed until it shines, and a chinaberry sapling planted beside it, a little crooked. "For the quarrels," {npc} says to you, very politely, as if you might answer. "It is a long walk up to the spring."

choices.text: Lie down under the straw roof

mem.note: came down to my yard

effects.log: The straw smells of summer. Children watch you over the wall in rows like sparrows. That evening, for the first time in years, nobody in the village tells a lie before supper.

choices.text: Keep the spring, and come down only on market days

effects.log: You come down on market days, lie in the yard from noon to dusk, and go back up to the cold water. {npc} keeps the straw fresh for you all the same. The sapling grows straighter than it was planted.

choices.text: Sniff the trough, and the headman, and go back up the hill

effects.log: The trough is clean. {npc} is mostly honest, except about the size of last year's harvest. You go home to the spring. A shelter in a yard is a kind of leash, even when it is made of straw and kindness.

events.text: The shared well at the bottom of the lane has gone foul: a dead rat in the bucket, and the water bitter with lye. Everybody knows who did it: the new family from over the pass, who keep to themselves and talk funny. The new family's father stands in the lane with his hands open, saying nothing in his funny accent. Behind the crowd, the miller's small son is crying very hard and will not say why.

choices.text: Walk past the new family and lie down beside the crying boy (the horn: true)

effects.log: The horn goes warm at the stranger and cold at the boy, but it is the cold of fear, not of malice: he dropped his mother's lye pot down the well chasing a rat. You lie down beside him and the crowd understands. Nobody beats him much. The new family is asked to supper.

choices.text: Lower your head at the boy before the whole lane

effects.log: You lower your head at a crying child. The lane gasps. It is the truth, and the miller beats him in the yard for it while you listen. The truth was owed. You are not sure the beating was.

choices.text: Lie down across the lane so nobody can reach the new family, and say nothing

effects.log: Nobody goes past a horned beast lying in a lane. The crowd mutters and goes home. The well is cleaned. The new family is never quite trusted, and the boy never quite stops looking at you. (-3 Clarity)

events.text: A betrothal goes wrong in the yard. The go-between, {npc}, a cheerful round person with a fan, swears that the bride's family promised an ox with the bride; the bride's family swears it was a calf; the groom's family swears it was an ox and two bolts of cloth. Everyone is shouting, the bride is sitting on a mat looking at the sky, and the go-between keeps glancing at you and fanning harder.

choices.text: Lower your head at the go-between (the horn: a lie)

effects.log: {npc} promised the ox to one family and the calf to the other, and meant to keep the difference. Your horn finds the fan first. Both families turn on {him} at once, and in the end, united by fury, the betrothal goes ahead.

choices.text: Lie down next to the bride on the mat and look at the sky too

effects.log: The bride glances at you. You both look at the sky. After a while the shouting stops, because people feel foolish shouting beside two calm creatures looking at clouds. The ox and the calf are both forgotten by spring.

choices.text: Look at each family in turn, very slowly

ok.log: Both families are telling the truth as they heard it. The fan, on the other hand, stops moving when you look at it. You lower your head at {npc}, and the yard goes quiet, and then very loud.

fail.log: The bride's uncle is sweating and shifty, and you lower your head at the uncle. The uncle was only ashamed that the family is poor. The go-between fans and smiles. Something in your horn cracks, very quietly. (A crack: -8 Clarity)

events.text: Years in the yard now, and the village has changed shape around you like water round a stone. Liars take the long way to the well, by the back lane, so as not to pass the shelter. The headman's grandchildren learned to walk holding your mane. The market in the next valley calls this the honest village, half as praise and half as a joke, and charges it less for salt.

choices.text: Stay. A village that keeps its own truth is worth a lifetime

effects.log: You stay, and grow, and the shelter is rebuilt twice around you. Somebody plants a second chinaberry. Nobody remembers who.

choices.text: Move to the crossroads outside the village, where strangers pass

effects.log: Strangers lie more than neighbours. By the end of your first month at the crossroads a horse thief, a false pilgrim and a salt merchant with a hollow weight have all turned back the way they came.

choices.text: Notice that the village has stopped thinking for itself

effects.log: A child asks you which of two paths to take. A woman asks you whether the rice is ready. You realise they bring you every question now, not only the lies. You start walking up to the spring for a week at a time, so they have to remember how.

events.text: A boy of about ten, {npc}, runs into the yard with a stick for a sword and a story: the old charcoal burner who lives alone at the edge of the wood stole the headman's hen. {npc} saw it, {he} says. {He} wants to be a hero. Half the village is behind {him}, and the charcoal burner, who is deaf, is being dragged in by the sleeve without the least idea why.

choices.text: Lie down at the charcoal burner's feet, ears back (the horn: true)

mem.note: took the burner's side, not mine

effects.log: The horn is warm at the old burner, all the way through. You lay your ears back and bow to the deaf old man, and the whole yard sees it. A fox took the hen; its feathers are found by the wood that evening. {npc} goes very red.

choices.text: Look at the boy until the story starts to wobble

ok.log: You look at {npc}. {npc} looks at you. "I did see someone," {he} says. "Somebody old. In the dark. It might have been a fox." The yard laughs. The burner is let go and given an egg for the trouble.

fail.log: The boy will not look at you, and the crowd takes that as proof against the burner. You have to lie across the gate all night so nobody goes after the deaf old man. In the morning a fox is seen with a red feather in its teeth.

choices.text: Lower your head, very gently, at the boy's stick

effects.log: You lower your horn at the stick, not the child. {npc} drops it as if it were hot. Heroes, you would tell {him} if you could speak, begin by being sure.

events.text: Two farmers, {npc} and a neighbour, and one brown ox with a white blaze, standing in the yard in the rain. Each swears the ox is their own, raised from a calf. Each describes the scar on its hind leg, the way it sulks at a heavy plough, the name it answers to. You lower your head toward the first and the horn is silent. You turn to the second. Silent. Neither is lying. Both believe it.

choices.text: Lie down between them, and stay lying down

effects.log: You lie down in the mud between them and do not lower your head at anyone. The yard waits. It is a long, wet wait. In the end the headman says, slowly, that perhaps there were two oxen once, and the old men begin to remember a calf that was sold.

choices.text: Nudge the ox out of the yard and see where it goes

ok.log: The ox ambles out of the gate, down the lane, and into a third farmer's byre, where it lies down with a sigh. The third farmer goes white. Two oxen, years ago, one sold and one strayed. Nobody lied. Everyone was wrong.

fail.log: The ox ambles into the headman's vegetable garden and eats the cabbages. Nobody remembers the quarrel for a week, which is a kind of result.

choices.text: Lower your head at one of them anyway: the village wants an answer

mem.note: called me a liar over my own ox

effects.log: You choose {npc}. The yard nods: the beast has spoken. {npc} looks at you as if you had kicked a child. Something in your horn cracks, very quietly. (A crack: -8 Clarity)

events.text: The headman comes to you at dusk with a jar of barley tea and a grievance. "They say you would not point," he says. "What use is a horn that does not point? The other village has a shaman who points at somebody every time. People like an answer."

choices.text: Turn your back and look at the hills

effects.log: He talks for a while to your back. Then he drinks the barley tea himself and goes home. You hear him tell his wife that the beast is stubborn, and that perhaps that is the point.

choices.text: Take him to the edge of the yard and lie down with your horn on the ground

effects.log: The horn on the earth, the ears back, the eyes on him. He looks at it a long time. "When you do not know," he says slowly, "you put it down." He goes home and tells it in the tavern as if it were his own idea. It becomes a village saying.

choices.text: Point at someone next time, so they keep believing

effects.log: You decide that a horn the village trusts is worth a little guessing. The horn, which was not consulted, feels heavier on your brow for the rest of the year. (-4 Clarity)

events.text: An old man, {npc}, insists before the yard that {he} paid {his} grain-loan back at the last harvest. {He} describes the day: the sacks, the clerk's brush, the cold. The clerk's book says {he} did not. The horn is silent on the old man. It is silent on the clerk, too. And the old man's daughter, standing behind {him}, will not meet anybody's eyes.

choices.text: Lie down beside the daughter and wait (the horn: true)

effects.log: The horn is warm all round: nobody is lying. The daughter tells it at last, crying: {npc} paid at the harvest two years ago, not last. {He} remembers the cold, and the sacks, and the wrong year. The daughter sold the rice to buy {his} medicine. The clerk lets the debt stand over a year. Nobody is butted.

choices.text: Do not lower your head at anyone

effects.log: The yard waits for a butt that does not come. The headman, who has learned, sends someone to look at the old man's storehouse. It is empty in a way that explains everything to everyone, eventually.

choices.text: Lower your head at the clerk. Clerks lie

effects.log: For once the clerk had not lied. The yard cheers. The clerk is pelted with mud on the way home and does not come back to this village for the next three harvests. Something in your horn cracks, very quietly. (A crack: -8 Clarity)

events.text: Snow on your back. You lie awake with the horn cold on your brow and think about the ox, and the old man and the wrong year. You were born knowing a lie the way a tongue knows salt. Nobody told you that most of what is false in the world is not a lie at all.

choices.text: Error is not a lie. Never lower your head at an honest mistake

effects.log: It goes into you the way the cold goes into stone. From now on, when the horn is silent, you will be silent too. It will cost you some answers. It will save you more cracks.

choices.text: A mistake can still do harm. Somebody must answer for it

effects.log: You decide the horn is for lies, but your weight is for harm. When an honest mistake floods a field, you will still stand in the flooder's doorway until they mend the dyke. That is not a butt. It is close.

events.text: Somebody has left you a bundle of chinaberry leaves on the trough, tied with straw, very fresh, very bitter, exactly what you like. Inside the leaves, rolled tight, there is a bar of silver. You know whose it is before you lift your head: {npc}, the steward of the biggest landowner in the valley, is leaning on the yard wall in a good silk coat, not looking at you. The landowner's case against three tenants comes to the yard next week.

choices.text: Carry the bundle in your mouth to the steward's gate and drop it there

effects.log: You walk the length of the village with a bar of silver in your teeth, and half the village follows to see where you are going. You drop it at the steward's gate. {npc} does not come out. Everybody knows anyway.

choices.text: Lower your head at the steward, in front of the whole village

mem.note: shamed me before the village

effects.log: You walk to the wall and lower your horn at {npc}'s good silk coat until {he} backs into a pig trough. Silver is a lie too: it says "this is fair" when it is not. The tenants hear about it before nightfall.

choices.text: Eat the leaves around the silver, and leave the silver where it is

mem.note: kept the silver

effects.log: You eat the leaves. The silver lies on the trough in the sun, and nobody touches it, because it is yours now. The bitterness is the same as always. Your horn, oddly, is not quite so cold the next morning. (-8 Clarity)

events.text: The landowner's case comes to the yard. Three tenant families, thin as reeds, are accused of hiding a fifth of the harvest. The landowner sits in person on a carried chair. The steward, {npc}, reads the accounts aloud in a fine clear voice, and glances at you after every line.

choices.text: Lower your head at the steward's accounts (the horn: a lie)

effects.log: The fine clear voice is lying in every second line: the "hidden fifth" went to the steward's own storehouse. You lower your horn at the paper in {npc}'s hands. The landowner turns slowly to look at the steward, and the tenants go home with their rice. The village will tell this one for a hundred years.

choices.text: Look at each of them, and judge as well as you can

ok.log: Under the fine voice there is a smell of new rice from the steward's own sleeves. You lower your head at {npc}. The landowner, who is not a fool, has the steward's storehouse opened before dark.

fail.log: The horn is a fog. You lie down and refuse to point. The landowner wins by default, the tenants pay, and that winter you hear children crying in the cold houses at the end of the valley.

choices.text: The horn is cloudy as river water. Lie down and say so

effects.log: You lay your horn on the ground before everyone: today it cannot see. The headman sends the case to the county town. It is not justice, but it is honest about not being justice.

choices.text: Lower your head at the tenants, as the silver asks

effects.log: You do it. Three thin families are put off their land before the snow. The silver on the trough is still bright; you will never be able to look at it again. Something in your horn cracks, very quietly. (A crack: -10 Clarity)

events.text: {npc} is back, older, in a better coat, with a new master and an old memory. {He} sits on the wall of the yard and talks to you quietly, the way people talk to a horse they are about to sell. "You took the silver once. You are the same beast. A little matter of a mill: next month. Nobody needs to be butted. You need only lie still."

choices.text: Get up, and go and lie down at the miller's door instead

effects.log: The whole village sees where you go. {npc} sits on the wall for a long time after you have left it, looking at the place where you used to be. The thread snaps. It is a relief to the horn.

choices.text: Lower your head at {npc} where {he} sits

mem.note: turned on me after I paid you

effects.log: {npc} goes over the wall backwards. That night a man with a net is asking at the inn which way the horned beast walks to water. Some debts are paid in silver, and some in hunters.

choices.text: Lie still, as asked

effects.log: You lie still at the mill case. The miller who was wronged looks at you all the time the judgement is read. A thread from your horn runs to a wall in a good coat, and every year it pulls a little tighter. (-8 Clarity)

events.text: Another bundle of chinaberry leaves on your trough, bitter and fresh, tied with straw. Another bar of silver inside. There is no note; there never is. A case is coming, and somebody would like you to remember who brings you the best leaves.

choices.text: Leave the silver on the road at the village gate for whoever needs it

effects.log: A widow finds it in the morning and buys seed rice. The giver hears where it went and does not try again for a while.

choices.text: Track the smell of the hand that tied it

ok.log: Silk, ink, ginseng tea: a county scribe. You lie down at the scribe's gate with the silver between your paws until the whole street has seen it. The case, when it comes, is very honestly argued.

fail.log: Too many hands have touched it. You drop the bundle in the stream and wash the taste out of your mouth.

choices.text: Keep it. The leaves are very good

effects.log: You eat the leaves and the silver stays. It is not much, you tell yourself. Your horn disagrees in the morning. (-8 Clarity)

events.text: A moneylender, {npc}, comes to the yard with a note: the widow at the end of the lane borrowed twenty sacks of rice from {him} and owes forty now, and here is the dead husband's mark on the paper to prove it. The widow swears the dead man never borrowed a grain in a whole life. The widow's son, tall, with a burn scar on one arm, says nothing at all, and that is worse.

choices.text: Lower your head at the note in {npc}'s hand (the horn: a lie)

effects.log: The paper is a lie. The horn goes cold the moment it is unrolled. You lower your head at it, not at {npc}, and {npc} snatches it back very fast. The note goes home in {his} sleeve, and the widow's son lets out a breath held for a month.

choices.text: Lower your head at the moneylender on your judgement

ok.log: {npc} smells of ink that is too new for a note three years old. You lower your head, and the yard sees {him} flinch. The widow keeps the rice.

fail.log: The horn will not say, and you will not guess. The headman sends the matter to the county. The county is slow. The son is not.

choices.text: Lie down beside the widow's son and watch

effects.log: The son smells of lamp oil and resolve. You lie beside the son all through the quarrel, and the son keeps glancing at you, and then at the moneylender's thatch. You know exactly what is meant, sooner or later.

events.text: Midnight. A torch moving down the lane toward the moneylender's house: the widow's son, with a jar of lamp oil under his arm and a face like a shut door. The moneylender's thatch is dry from a month without rain, and the houses on either side are thatched too.

choices.text: Stand in the lane in front of him

ok.log: He tries to go round you. You are wider than the lane. He tries to go over the wall, and you are there. In the end he sits down in the dust and weeps, and you lie down beside him until the torch goes out.

fail.log: He swings the torch at your face and the fire catches your mane. You roll in the ditch; he runs past. But your roaring has woken the lane, and twenty people are standing in front of the thatch when he gets there. (-8 health)

choices.text: Wake the whole lane with a bellow

effects.log: Every door opens. The son stands in the middle of the lane with a torch and a jar of oil and fifty eyes on him. He goes home. Nobody speaks of it, ever, which is a mercy of its own.

choices.text: Let him. The moneylender is a liar

effects.log: You lie in the yard and let the torch go by. The moneylender's house burns, and the house next door, where a family of five was asleep. They get out. Their ox does not. A haechi does not let fire judge. You know that now. (-5 Clarity)

events.text: The moneylender is back with a new note and a scribe, {npc}, a thin young person with ink on every finger. The moneylender is angry and honest-sounding. The scribe is very calm. When you lower your head toward the moneylender this time, the horn is not quite cold. When you turn toward the scribe, it is ice.

choices.text: Lower your head at the scribe (the horn: a lie)

effects.log: The scribe forged the first note, too, and the moneylender believed it: the scribe meant to collect the forty sacks and keep twenty. The moneylender sits down in the yard looking old. A liar, it turns out, can also be lied to.

choices.text: Let it go: the scribe is very young, and very hungry

effects.log: You lie down and let the case go unanswered. The note is not paid; nobody is punished. Later you see the scribe at the spring, washing ink off their hands for a long time. (-3 Clarity)

choices.text: Follow the coldness, wherever it is strongest

ok.log: You turn from the moneylender to the calm young scribe and lower your head. {npc} goes on being calm for a breath too long. Then the ink-stained hands start to shake.

fail.log: You lower your head at the moneylender, because you did last time. This time it was not the moneylender. Something in your horn cracks, very quietly. (A crack: -8 Clarity)

events.text: Twenty years on. The widow is long buried under a mound on the hill. Her son is an elder of the village now, grey at the temples, the burn scar still on his arm. He brings his grandson to the shelter and sits the boy down in front of you. "This is the one," he tells the child, "who stood in the lane."

choices.text: Lay your ears back and bow to the old man

effects.log: He bows back, slowly, the way the old do. The grandson looks from one of you to the other and does not understand yet. He will.

choices.text: Nudge the boy's hand with your nose

effects.log: The boy giggles and grabs your mane, and the old man laughs too, for the first time in your hearing. The scar on his arm is only a scar now.

events.text: The one you lowered your head at, {npc}, cannot buy salt in the market any more. Children throw stones at the gate. Somebody has written a word in mud on the wall that the rain has not quite washed off. Everybody knows: the beast pointed. Only you know that the horn was silent, and you guessed.

choices.text: Go and lie down at {npc}'s gate, in front of everybody

effects.log: The beast who pointed is lying at the gate it pointed at. The stones stop. The village does not understand, and grumbles, and slowly begins to wonder. {npc} does not come out. But the next morning there is a bowl of water by the gate.

choices.text: Go back to where you pointed, and lower your horn to the ground before everybody

effects.log: You lay your horn in the dust where you pointed and keep it there until everyone nearby has come to look. It takes them a long time to understand that a beast can say "I was wrong". Some never do. The stones stop.

choices.text: Stay away. Showing yourself would only make it worse

effects.log: You stay away. The stones do not stop. You hear them from the spring at night, one, then another, like rain beginning.

events.text: Dawn, and a handcart in the lane: {npc}'s family is leaving. Pots, a rolled mat, a grandmother perched on the bundles, a dog that does not understand. Nobody from the village comes out to say goodbye. They know where the cart is going only as far as the bend.

choices.text: Walk behind the cart to the next valley, all the way

effects.log: Three days behind a handcart. Bandits look at the cart, and at you, and go away. At the end there is a hamlet that does not know them, and a hut with a hole in the roof. You know where they are now. That will matter. (-5 health)

choices.text: Stand at the bend and watch them out of sight

effects.log: The grandmother looks back once from the top of the bundles. Then the cart goes round the bend, and the lane is empty, and you are standing in it.

choices.text: Lie down across the lane so the cart cannot pass: they should stay, and you should mend it here

ok.log: The cart stops. The neighbours come out to see why, and see the beast lying in the lane with its horn on the ground before a family it pointed at. Something shifts. The headman helps unload the cart. It is not forgiveness. It is room for it.

fail.log: {npc} takes the dog and the grandmother and goes round you through the paddies, and the cart is left in the lane. Nobody takes it in. It is still there in the spring, falling apart, and every time you pass it you remember.

events.text: A crack in a horn is not a wound that hurts. It is a kind of quiet. Where there was a clean cold note when a lie came near, there is now, sometimes, nothing. You lie awake listening to it, the way a bell-maker listens to a bell with a flaw.

choices.text: Shake your head, hard, and listen to the ring

effects.log: It rings, almost true. Under the ring, very faint, there is a buzz, like a fly in a jar. You will hear that buzz every time from now on. It is the sound of a guess.

choices.text: Swear never to guess again

effects.log: When the horn is silent, you will lie down. You swear it to the spring at night. It is a hard oath for a beast that people bring their quarrels to.

choices.text: Go and find the bitter leaf, and eat it until your mouth is numb

effects.log: A season of bitterness. The quiet in the horn is still there in the spring, but the rest of it rings clearer around it.

events.text: Years later, and far from the village. A hut in a hamlet you once followed a handcart to, and beside it a grave mound with the grass grown long. {npc}, a grandchild of the family you wronged, is cutting the grass with a sickle and talking to the mound, as people do.

choices.text: Lie down at the edge of the grave and wait

mem.note: came to grandfather's grave

effects.log: {npc} sees you and goes very still. Then {he} goes on cutting the grass, slower. "Grandmother said you would come," {he} says, to the grave and not to you. "Grandmother said you looked sorry. Grandmother said it did not help."

choices.text: Cut the grass yourself, with your teeth, the whole mound

effects.log: It takes all afternoon and your mouth is green and bleeding a little. {npc} watches from the hut door and does not help and does not stop you. When you are done there is a cup of water on the step. (-3 health)

events.text: {npc}, grown now, sits on the step of the hut beside the grave and looks at you for a long time. "They spat the word after Grandmother until the day Grandmother died," {he} says. "Not loudly. Just wherever the story had travelled. You know what I want? I want you to go back to that village and tell them. Out loud. In the yard."

choices.text: Go back to the village yard, and lower your horn to the earth before them all, every market day for a year

mem.note: went and said it in the yard

effects.log: A year of market days with your horn in the dust. By the end, the children who repeat the word are the grandchildren of the ones who first spat it, and they stop, and ask their grandparents why. Some of the old ones are ashamed. It is late. It is not nothing.

choices.text: Lay your ears back and stay here instead, by the grave, for a season

effects.log: {npc} wanted the village told, not a beast at a grave. But {he} brings you water every morning anyway, and on the last day {he} says the grave looks better kept than it has in years.

events.text: The crack in your horn has a direction. You can feel it, the way a dowser feels water: it points back along the road toward {npc}, the one you wronged. Not toward forgiveness. Toward a person, who owes you nothing, and who may still be angry, and is entitled to be.

choices.text: Follow it, however far

effects.log: Three provinces of roads. You learn the way a crack points: weakly in the rain, strongly at dusk. At the end there is a gate. (-5 health)

choices.text: Not yet. You are not ready to be refused

effects.log: You stay at the spring. The crack keeps pointing. It is very patient.

events.text: The gate the crack led you to is shut. Behind it, {npc} knows exactly what is lying outside, and has not opened it in nine days. On the tenth day the gate opens a hand's width and a voice says, very quietly: "Forgiveness is not owed. Go away."

choices.text: Go away, as asked

effects.log: You go. It is the right thing and it does not mend anything, and both of those are true. On the road you understand that the asking was for you, and the refusing was for them, and they were right to keep it.

choices.text: Lie down again. A season, and then go

effects.log: You lie outside the gate through a season of rain. {npc} never opens it. On the last day there is a bowl of water outside it, which may mean something, or may only be water. (-6 health)

events.text: You find {npc} at last, mending a fence in a village two valleys from the one where you pointed. {He} straightens up, sees the horn, and does not run. The village has been told about the beast that points, and is watching.

choices.text: Stay at the gate until you are asked in, or sent away

mem.note: asked my forgiveness, and had it

ok.log: For a whole season you lie by the fence while {npc} mends it, and pass {him} the posts in your teeth. One evening {he} says, "You were wrong," and you lay your ears back, and {he} nods, and that is all. The crack in your horn closes.

fail.log: {npc} throws a fence post at you and goes indoors. Fair. (-8 health)

choices.text: Leave something useful at the gate, and go

ok.log: You lie at the foot of the dyer's stairs for a season, blue and red dye on your paws. One morning {npc} comes down with a bowl of water. "They bow to you in the town," {he} says. "I wanted you to come to me." You did. The crack in your horn closes.

events.text: In the capital, among ten thousand people, the crack in your horn finds one: {npc}, who sells straw sandals by the South Gate and has never forgotten the day you lowered your head at the wrong one. You can speak now. That makes it harder.

ok.log: You sit by the sandal mat every day for a season and say, every day, the same three words. On the last day {npc} gives you a pair of sandals much too small for any paw. "For your human shape," {he} says. "If you ever have one. Walk somewhere honest in them." The crack in your horn closes.

ok.log: You bring the file in your teeth and lay it on {npc}'s step, and lie down beside it while {he} burns it page by page. When the last page is ash, {he} puts a hand on your horn, very lightly, on the crack, and holds it there. The crack in your horn closes.

fail.log: {npc} reads the file, then reads it aloud to you, every line, in a flat voice, and shuts the door. You lie outside it all night with every line in your ears. (-8 health)

events.text: A farmer comes to the yard alone at night, so nobody will see. His newborn does not look like him: grey eyes, when the whole family is brown-eyed. The pedlar who sold needles last spring had grey eyes. He wants you to look at his wife in the morning and tell the village the truth. The village keeps the old ways about such things.

choices.text: Lower the horn. Lie still in the morning and look at nothing

effects.log: In the morning you look at the hills. The farmer stands in the yard waiting for a butt that never comes, and finally takes it as an answer, the kind he wants. He goes home and holds the baby. Whatever was true stays in your horn, and stays heavy. (-3 Clarity)

choices.text: Look at the wife in the morning, as asked

ok.log: The horn goes warm at her, all the way through. Grey eyes come up in families like rocks come up in fields; her own grandfather had them, she says, and the old women of the village remember it once they are asked. The farmer weeps with relief. You were sure, this time.

fail.log: The horn will not say, and the whole village is watching you not say it. Silence, in that yard, is taken as a verdict. You have to lie across the farmer's gate for a month to keep the family safe from their neighbours.

choices.text: Go and look at the baby first, alone

effects.log: You put your nose to the baby, and the baby grabs your mane and laughs. A haechi cannot tell a child's father by looking. It can tell that a child is a child. In the morning you lie down beside the cradle and stay there, and the village draws its own conclusion: the beast has claimed it. Nobody touches that family.

events.text: A soldier, {npc}, has come home from the northern border with a bandaged arm and a story: wounded in the skirmish at the river, sent home by the captain. The family hangs a lantern for joy. Your horn goes cold. {npc} fled. If the garrison learns it, {npc} will be flogged, and the family's name will be mud for three generations.

choices.text: Lower the horn, and let the lantern burn

effects.log: You lie still under the lantern. {npc} sees you not pointing, and understands that you know. {He} does not sleep that night. The next spring {he} goes back to the border on {his} own, without being sent. (-3 Clarity)

choices.text: Lower your head at {npc}, as the horn says

mem.note: told on me

effects.log: The lantern is taken down. {npc} is taken to the county town in the morning and comes back with a back that will scar. The family does not look at you for years. It was true. It was all true.

choices.text: Stare at {npc} until {he} says it {him}self

ok.log: {npc} breaks before supper and tells the family. It is better, somehow, said than found. The headman, who also ran once, a long time ago, makes sure the garrison hears only that a soldier was sent home.

fail.log: {npc} stares back. A soldier who ran from a battle does not run from a beast. The lie stays in the house, and you leave it there.

events.text: The village shrine's offering bowl was robbed of its copper in the night. The elders say the thief must be driven out of the valley in winter, as the old custom says. Your horn has already found the thief: a girl of thirteen whose little brother has the coughing fever, who bought him a root of medicine at the market this morning.

choices.text: Lower the horn. The copper is in a sick child

effects.log: You lie still while the elders question everyone. Nobody is driven out. The brother lives. The shrine is short of copper, and somebody quietly puts it back over the next year in single coins, one each market day. (-3 Clarity)

choices.text: Go to the shrine and lower your head at the bowl itself

effects.log: You lower your head at the empty bowl and keep it there until the elders understand: the theft is real, the thief is not to be named. The elders argue all night. In the end they decide the mountain spirit took it as a fee, and leave it at that.

choices.text: Lower your head at the girl, and then lie down in front of her

effects.log: The truth first, and then your body between her and the elders. Nobody drives a child out of the valley past a horned beast. The custom bends; it has bent before. The girl sweeps the shrine for a year instead.

events.text: You count the truths you have kept to yourself. A child's eyes. A soldier's arm. A copper in a medicine root. Each one sits in the horn like a stone in a shoe. A haechi is for seeing. What is a haechi that sees, and says nothing?

choices.text: Something kind. Silence is not always a lie

effects.log: You decide that the horn owes the world the truth about the guilty, and nothing about the merely sad. It is a line you will walk for a thousand years, and you will not always find it.

choices.text: Something dangerous. Every hidden thing is dry wood

effects.log: You do not know yet about the mountain shaped like flame. But you know already that a truth kept is a thing kept somewhere, and things kept somewhere can catch. You will lower the horn more rarely.

events.text: A shaman, {npc}, has come over the pass with a drum, a fan, a bundle of coloured robes and a terrible news: the spirit of the village well is angry, and will dry it up unless three sacks of rice are offered at the next full moon, to be carried away afterwards by the shaman for the proper rites. The village is frightened. It was a dry summer.

choices.text: Lower your head at the shaman in the middle of the rite (the horn: a lie)

mem.note: ruined my rite

effects.log: The drum stops. The fan stops. The bells go on a little by themselves. {npc} looks at the horn lowered at {his} heart and says, very quickly, that the spirit has changed its mind and one sack will do. The village keeps all three.

choices.text: Go and lie down beside the well, on the spirit's side

effects.log: The village sees the horned beast lying calmly at the well with its head on the stones, and decides the spirit is not angry with anybody. {npc} dances the whole rite to a crowd that is no longer listening and leaves with half a sack.

choices.text: Watch the rite to the end, and judge it on its merits

ok.log: At the height of the rite {npc} says the spirit speaks through {him}. Your horn goes cold at every word in the spirit's voice and warm at none. You lower your head. The village carries its rice home.

fail.log: The drumming gets into your head and the horn goes muddy. Three sacks go over the pass on a mule. The well does not dry up. The shaman, naturally, takes the credit.

events.text: In the next village an old shaman, {npc}, tiny and bent, sits beside a dying old woman's mat, holding the old hand. The old woman's son went to sea two winters ago and never came back; everybody knows the boat went down. The old woman asks whether the son will come home. {npc} says, gently, that the boat is on its way, and that it is time to rest until it comes.

choices.text: Lower the horn and lie down outside the door

effects.log: The old woman dies in the night, smiling, waiting for a boat. {npc} comes out at dawn and sits beside you on the step. "You heard," {he} says. You did. Neither of you says anything else. (-3 Clarity)

choices.text: Lower your head at the shaman's words. A lie is a lie

effects.log: The horn finds the lie and you lower your head at it, at the bedside. The dying woman sees the beast pointing and understands. The weeping for the lost son goes on all night, and ends in the morning with the life. The truth was owed to someone. You are no longer sure it was owed to that bed.

choices.text: Go in and lay your head on the dying woman's mat

effects.log: You say nothing about the son. You only lie beside the mat, very warm, and an old hand comes into your mane, and talks to you all night about the son: what the boy ate, how the boy laughed. By morning the goodbye has been said without anyone asking for it.

events.text: The false shaman, {npc}, is back, with a better robe and a proposal. {He} squats by the yard wall and talks low. "You and me, beast. I do the rites, you lie at the well and look wise. Every third sack is yours: rolled in the bitterest leaves you ever ate. The villages are happy. Who is hurt?"

choices.text: Follow {npc} to the next village and lie down at the well before {he} gets there

effects.log: Every village {npc} comes to has a horned beast already lying at its well, calm as a stone. By the fifth village {he} has stopped unpacking the drum.

choices.text: Lower your head at {him} where {he} squats

effects.log: {npc} falls over backwards into the ditch, robe and all. The yard laughs. Laughter is a very good cure for a frightening shaman.

choices.text: Accept: who is hurt?

effects.log: A season of rites. You lie at wells looking wise, and villages give rice they cannot spare to spirits that were never angry. The leaves are very bitter. They do not help. (-8 Clarity)

events.text: The old shaman of the next village, {npc}, sends for you before {he} dies. {He} looks at you a long time from the mat, with eyes that see more than eyes should. "I will tell you a true thing about yourself," {he} says, "in exchange for the one you heard me say."

choices.text: Lie down and listen

effects.npcPass: old age, a shaman who saw true
effects.log: "You will sit before a gate one day," {npc} says, "and look at a mountain that wants to burn. And everything you have kept quiet will be lying under the roofs behind you like straw." {He} closes {his} eyes. You do not understand it. You will.

choices.text: Lay your ears back and bow, and go without hearing it

effects.npcPass: old age, a shaman who saw true
effects.log: A shaman's last truth should go to somebody who will be here tomorrow. You bow and go. Behind you, {npc} laughs, very softly, and calls you a good beast.

events.text: The children in the lane are playing haechi. One of them, {npc}, has a paper horn tied to {his} forehead with a hair ribbon and walks on all fours, very solemnly, between the others. They tell lies at {him} on purpose. {npc} butts the liars in the stomach with the paper horn. Then {he} stops in front of the biggest boy, the one who breaks everybody's tops, and points.

choices.text: Nod, very slowly, from where you lie (the horn: true)

effects.log: The big boy did break the tops. The whole lane sees the real beast nod at the paper one, and the big boy gives everybody's tops back by evening. {npc} wears the paper horn for a month.

choices.text: Get up and walk over and lie down next to the paper haechi

effects.log: Two haechi, one real and one paper, lying side by side in the lane. The big boy looks from one horn to the other and does the arithmetic. {npc} is a hero for a week.

choices.text: Stay out of it: let them have their game

effects.log: You let them play. The big boy denies everything; the paper haechi butts the big boy anyway; there is a fight; everybody goes home muddy. Children's courts are rougher than yours, and quicker.

events.text: The big boy's father comes to the gate with his son by the ear, red with anger. "My son says the beast pointed at him because a little brat with a paper hat told it to. Since when does a haechi take orders from children?"

choices.text: Lower your head at the big boy's pockets

effects.log: Two tops fall out of the boy's pockets, painted in other children's colours. The father looks at them for a long time and goes home with his son by the other ear.

choices.text: Lay your ears back to the father: he is an honest man, angry for his son

effects.log: He did not expect a bow. It takes the wind out of him. He goes home and asks his son some questions, more quietly, and gets some answers.

events.text: Years later, a young runner of the magistrate's office in a blue jacket stops in front of you with a tied bundle under one arm, out of breath. You know the smell under the ink and sweat: {npc}, the child with the paper horn. "I kept the horn," {he} says, though you cannot answer. "I still have it. This is the clerk's second ledger. Somebody has to show it to someone."

choices.text: Take the bundle in your teeth and carry it to the magistrate's hall

mem.note: carried the ledger for me

effects.log: A horned beast walking up the steps of the hall with a ledger in its jaws. Nobody stops you. The magistrate unties it in front of the whole yard, and the county clerk sits down very suddenly on the steps.

choices.text: Lie down on top of the bundle and wait for the right day

effects.log: A ledger produced on the wrong day is a dead runner. You lie on it in the yard for a month, and nobody dares to ask you to move, and {npc} waits, nervous and proud, until the governor's inspector comes through.

events.text: A palanquin in the village lane, and runners in blue jackets, and a county magistrate, {npc}, who gets down panting and looks at you the way a buyer looks at a horse. "I have read the old books," {he} says to the headman. "In ancient times a beast like this sat in the courts and pointed at the guilty, and the judges never had to think at all. My court is very busy." {He} has brought a cart.

choices.text: Climb into the cart

effects.log: The headman weeps a little. The village children run behind the cart to the end of the valley. The county town is bigger and dirtier and louder than anything you have seen, and every third person in it is lying about something.

choices.text: Walk beside the cart instead. A haechi is not carried

effects.log: You walk the whole road beside the empty cart. The runners are offended, the magistrate is amused, and the roadside villages remember it: the beast walked, and the magistrate rode.

choices.text: Lie down and refuse. The village is not finished

effects.log: {npc} tries for a whole afternoon: rice, threats, a scroll from the governor. You lie in the yard. In the end {he} goes away and says that it will come. You think {he} may be right.

events.text: The magistrate's courtyard: stone steps, a hall with a tiled roof, petitioners kneeling on straw mats in rows, and on the wall beside the steps an old painting, half flaked away, of a judge in robes and a beast with one horn. This morning there are fourteen cases. {npc} sits on the hall's porch, gestures at the first petitioner, and closes {his} eyes. "Point," {he} says.

choices.text: Work through all fourteen, slowly, and lie down when the horn is silent

effects.log: Fourteen cases, a whole day. Nine butts, five times lying down. By evening your horn aches the way an eye aches after reading by bad light. {npc} wakes up and is pleased with nine. The five {he} sends to be judged properly, grumbling. (-2 Clarity)

choices.text: Do three, then lie down and refuse the rest

effects.log: Three cases. Then you lie down with your back to the porch. {npc} is furious, then puzzled, then, after a while, begins to hear the other eleven {him}self. A horn that can be worn out can be lent out. You are not that horn.

choices.text: Point quickly at all fourteen, to please {him}

ok.log: Fourteen points before noon. By the luck of a fool, every one was right. {npc} is overjoyed and orders a stone trough for you. Your horn feels like it has been sanded. (-4 Clarity)

fail.log: Fourteen points before noon. Twelve were right. One was half right. One was a frightened porter who had done nothing at all, and is flogged in the yard while you listen. Something in your horn cracks, very quietly. (A crack: -8 Clarity)

events.text: At night the courtyard is empty, and you lie looking at the painting on the wall. The judge is a tall shape in a robe with a face too flaked to read. The beast beside him has a single horn, and the painter has given it the wrong ears, standing up like a dog's. It is looking at the judge, not at the guilty. That, you think, is the mistake.

choices.text: Lie down under the painted beast, ears laid back, facing the gate

effects.log: From then on, petitioners in that court come in to two beasts: one on the wall looking at the judge, and one on the stones looking at them. The old people say the painted one's ears look flatter every year.

choices.text: Rub your shoulder along the wall until the painted horn is clean of dust

effects.log: A night's work. In the morning the painted horn is white again, and a clerk swears that it was glowing when he came in. Clerks swear many things. Your horn agrees with that one.

events.text: The magistrate's own case comes to the courtyard in a closed sedan: {npc}'s nephew, accused of sinking a ferryman's boat for sport. The nephew stands on the steps in silk, bored. {npc} sits on the porch with {his} eyes open for once. "Point," {he} says, and looks at you very hard.

choices.text: Lower your head at the nephew (the horn: a lie)

effects.log: The silk stops looking bored. {npc} closes {his} eyes for a long time. Then {he} opens them and sentences {his} own nephew to pay for the ferry twice over. "That is what I brought you for," {he} says afterwards, to nobody. "I did not know it until now."

choices.text: Judge it as you would any other

ok.log: You lower your head at the silk. {npc} looks at you, then at the nephew, then at the wall painting, and pronounces the sentence in a voice like a door closing.

fail.log: The horn is uncertain, and you lie down. {npc} lets out a breath and sends the case to the governor, where it is lost for years.

choices.text: Lie down. This is not a quarrel; it is a test of the magistrate

effects.log: You refuse to point, and look at {npc} instead. The yard looks at {npc} too. In the end the magistrate has to decide it with {his} own eyes for once. {He} decides it rightly. You never quite know whether {he} would have without everybody looking.

events.text: {npc} has served out the term, and a new magistrate's palanquin is coming up the road. {npc} sits on the steps with you, in travelling clothes. "The new one is a scholar," {he} says. "One who thinks you are a superstition, and will have you put out of the yard. You should go somewhere bigger, where they need you more. The capital is that way."

choices.text: Walk out of the gate before the new palanquin comes in

effects.log: You go out by the side gate as the new magistrate comes in by the front. The courtyard is quieter after. The painted beast on the wall goes on looking at the judge.

choices.text: Stay, and let the new magistrate test you

ok.log: The new magistrate puts a test to you on the first day: three cases already solved. You get all three right. The scholar goes away and reads for a week, and comes back, and asks you to stay.

fail.log: The new magistrate has you driven out with brooms. Runners who used to bow to you bang pans. It is undignified. You walk south out of the town with straw in your mane.

choices.text: Lay your ears back to {npc} for the years in the yard

effects.log: {npc} laughs, embarrassed, and puts a hand on your horn as if it were a dog's head. "I learned to think," {he} says. "Don't tell anybody." You will not. You cannot.

events.text: The magistrate signs; the clerk writes. {npc}, the county's chief clerk, whose family has kept the county's books for nine generations, is a small, polite person who bows to you every morning exactly as deep as to the magistrate. Everything in the county goes through {his} brush: the land tax, the grain loans, the household registers. When {npc} bows, your horn goes cold, every morning, like ice on a pond.

choices.text: Bow back, and watch

effects.log: You bow back. {npc} smiles. Two very polite creatures, each knowing exactly what the other is. You start lying in the doorway of the records room at night.

choices.text: Lower your head at {npc} at once, in the yard

ok.log: You lower your head at the clerk on the steps. {npc} goes on smiling, and then explains to the magistrate, very reasonably, that the beast must be confused by the smell of the ink. The magistrate believes {him}. A butt is not proof. You need the ledger.

fail.log: You lower your head and {npc} only bows lower, and the magistrate laughs. You have told the clerk what you know, and the clerk has told you nothing.

choices.text: Follow {npc} home at night

effects.log: {npc} walks home by a long road past the grain store, stops, looks at the doors, and walks on. In {his} sleeve, something thick and square knocks against {his} hip at every step. Two books, not one.

events.text: Tax day. Farmers queue in the courtyard with sacks on their backs. {npc} weighs each sack, writes in the book, and sends them away. You lie by the scales and watch: an old woman's sack is weighed twice, and written down once. A young farmer's is written as short. The queue goes on all day, and nobody complains, because who would they complain to?

choices.text: Lower your head at {npc}'s sleeve, where the second book is (the horn: a lie)

effects.log: You put your horn against the sleeve and push, very gently. The second ledger falls out onto the stones and opens: every sack weighed twice and written once, nine generations of it. The courtyard goes silent, and then a thousand farmers begin to shout.

choices.text: Lie down on the scales so nothing can be weighed

effects.log: A beast on the scales. Nothing is weighed all afternoon. The farmers go home with their sacks, and the magistrate, called down at last, is made to look at the scales and the books for the first time in years. The magistrate does not find the second book. But the next tax day, the weights are honest.

choices.text: Watch the scales until you are sure, then point

ok.log: By the hundredth sack you are sure. You lower your head at {npc} in front of the queue, and keep it lowered until the magistrate comes down the steps and asks the clerk to empty both sleeves.

fail.log: The numbers go round and round in your head like millstones. Before you are sure, the day is over and the sacks are in the store.

events.text: {npc} comes to the records room at night where you lie, and sits on the floor in front of you with a lamp, a bundle of chinaberry leaves and a small sack that clinks. "My family has kept these books for nine generations," {he} says. "The magistrates come and go every three years. I am the county. Lie still for one more tax day."

choices.text: Knock the lamp over onto the second ledger

effects.log: The ledger burns, and so does the record of nine generations of theft, and the proof with it. {npc} beats out the flames with {his} sleeves, weeping. A haechi does not let fire judge. You knew that, and you did it anyway. (-3 Clarity)

choices.text: Lie still and look at {npc} until the lamp burns out

effects.log: {npc} talks for a long time, about the family, the debts, the magistrates who took their own share. Then the lamp burns out, and in the dark {he} says, "No, then." You hear the sack clink as {he} goes.

choices.text: Take the bundle

effects.log: The leaves are bitter and the silver is heavy, and the next tax day you lie by the scales with your eyes shut. It is the longest day you have ever spent. (-8 Clarity)

events.text: A beggar in a torn hat comes into the courtyard, sits on the steps, and opens his jacket to show a bronze tablet with horses cut into it: the king's secret inspector. The runners fall flat. He asks for the county's books, all of them, and then looks at you. "They say in the villages," he says, "that there is a beast in this yard who has known everything for years. Why did it never tell?"

choices.text: Walk to the records room and lie down in front of the hidden chest

effects.log: He opens the chest. Inside, the magistrate's private accounts, some letters from the governor, and whatever is left of the clerk's second book. The secret inspector sits down on the floor to read, and is still reading at dawn.

choices.text: Lay your horn on the ground before him: you told, and nobody listened

effects.log: He looks at the horn in the dust, and at the faded painting on the wall, and seems to understand. "A beast can only point," he says. "Somebody has to want to see." He writes that in his report. It is the only line of it that is ever quoted.

events.text: The river road south ends at a wall. It climbs over the hills on both sides as far as you can see, grey stone with a tiled cap. The road goes through a great gate under a double roof, and the gate's name plaque is hung on end, upright, not across like every plaque you have ever seen. A thousand people are pushing through it. Beyond the walls, far to the south across another river, there is a mountain whose peaks stand up like flames.

choices.text: Walk in through the gate at dawn, with the crowds

effects.log: The crowd parts round you like water round a rock and closes again behind. Nobody in the capital looks twice at anything for long. Inside: smoke, bells, ten thousand roofs, and more lies in one street than in a whole county. Your horn rings faintly all day, like a bell in a wind.

choices.text: Lie down outside the gate for a season first, and listen to the city

effects.log: A season outside the wall, watching who goes in and who comes out. You learn the gate's liars by their walk: the tax runners, the smugglers with salt in their hems, the scholars who have failed the examination three times and tell their families it is next year. Then you go in.

choices.text: Ask the gate guard why the plaque hangs on end

effects.log: You cannot ask. You sit and look up at it until the guard, uncomfortable, tells you anyway: it is turned on end so that it looks like a flame, and a flame facing a flame stands it off. "Against that," he says, and points south, at the mountain. Then he lets you in without the toll, and is not sure why.

events.text: In the yard of a tavern by the river gate, half buried in weeds, there is a stone haechi. Not a statue: it was a haechi once. When you lie down beside it at dusk, the stone opens one eye. "Another one," it says, in a voice like gravel. "Come about the mountain? Everybody comes about the mountain, sooner or later."

choices.text: Ask why a palace would face a mountain made of fire

effects.log: The old one tells it slowly. When the city was founded, a monk said the palace should face east, away from the fire, with the rock mountain at its back. A minister said a king must face south, as kings always have. The minister won. "Were they lying?" you ask. "Neither," says the stone. "That was the trouble. Both told the truth, and the king had to choose which fire to live with."

choices.text: Ask what the old one saw, sitting here

effects.log: "Lies," says the stone. "Every one that went through that gate. They do not go away, you know. They go under the roofs and dry out. And one day the mountain sends a spark." It closes its eye. "I sat here so long I stopped seeing them. Do not sit here so long."

choices.text: Lie quietly beside it and say nothing

effects.log: You lie beside the old stone until the moon is up. Once it sighs. Once, very faintly, the horn on its worn brow rings, the way yours does. In the morning it is only stone again.

events.text: From the top of the hill inside the north wall you can see the whole capital at once: the palace with its back to the rock mountain and its face to the south, the main road running down from its gate, ten thousand tiled and thatched roofs, and beyond the river the mountain shaped like flame, its peaks red in the evening sun. The wind is from the northwest. It smells of dry straw.

choices.text: Look at the Fire Mountain until it is dark

effects.log: It does not move. It does not need to. You feel it the way you feel a lie: a coldness at the tip of the horn. Not yet, it says, or you think it says. You do not belong at the palace gate yet. You will.

choices.text: Look at the roofs instead

effects.log: So many roofs, and under every roof, people, and among the people, the things they have not said. The straw smell of the wind and the smell of the roofs are the same smell. You do not know why that frightens you.

events.text: Your first winter inside the walls. The city's air is thick: every street has a merchant swearing to his weights, every gate a runner swearing to his errand, every tavern a scholar swearing to his learning. Your horn is never quiet. And everywhere there are sweet things: honey cakes left on your path, persimmons, rice candy, offered by people who would like you to be a little less sharp.

choices.text: Walk out past the wall every day for the bitter leaf

effects.log: An hour out, an hour back, every day of the winter, for leaves from the four chinaberry trees on the south slope. The city laughs at the beast that walks so far for something so nasty. The horn stays clean.

choices.text: Eat a honey cake. Just one

effects.log: It is the best thing you have ever tasted. The next morning a merchant tells you his weights are honest, and you believe him for a moment, before the horn wakes up. (-3 Clarity)

choices.text: Sleep under the drum tower by the palace, where it is quietest at night

effects.log: The drum hangs above you on the gate tower, silent. The guards get used to you. In the small hours, when even the liars sleep, the city is almost clean.

events.text: Three men with nets and short spears and a mule carrying a stone mortar, asking at every inn which road the horned beast takes to water. A horn that knows lies, ground fine and stirred into tea, is worth a governor's house to the right buyer. You smell them a day before they find you.

choices.text: Lead them into the marsh and lose them

ok.log: Three days of reeds and mud. You walk in circles round them until they are lost and furious with each other, and then you walk out. They go home with a cold, a broken net and a story nobody believes.

fail.log: A net in the reeds you did not smell. You tear through it, but the spear finds your flank on the way out. (-12 health)

choices.text: Walk out and stand in front of them on the road

ok.log: They throw the net. You walk through it. They throw the spears. You walk through those too, and stand over the three of them with your horn lowered, and they find that they have urgent business in another province.

fail.log: Three men who do this for a living. You get away with the net still round your back leg and a spear-cut on your brow, a finger from the horn. (-25 health)
fail.deathCause: the nets and spears of horn hunters on a riverbank

choices.text: Lie very still in the stream with only your horn above water

effects.log: They walk past a stick in the water three times. Hunters are honest about one thing: what they are looking for. You are not it, today.

events.text: A pilgrim, {npc}, with a staff and a gourd and a very new straw hat, sits down beside you at the ford and says {he} is going to the temple in the mountains to pray for a sick parent. Every word is soft and kind. Your horn goes cold at the gourd. There is something in it that is not water.

choices.text: Knock the gourd out of {npc}'s hand (the horn: a lie)

effects.log: It breaks on a stone and the ford fills with the smell of sleeping draught. {npc} looks at the spilled gourd, and then at you, and then runs, leaving the very new hat floating downstream.

choices.text: Drink from the ford upstream, away from {him}

effects.log: You move upstream. {npc} sighs, very quietly, the sigh of a person whose plan has just floated away, and offers you the gourd anyway. You do not take it.

choices.text: Take a drink from the offered gourd: the pilgrim seems kind

effects.log: The world goes slow and soft. You wake in a net in a cart, with three men arguing over who gets to hold the mortar, and break the cart apart getting out. (-15 health)

events.text: Men with nets again, on a road outside the capital: a whole crew this time, and a sedan chair at the back with its curtain drawn. Somebody rich wants a horn.

choices.text: Go into the city and lie down at the busiest gate, among the crowds

effects.log: Nobody throws a net in front of a thousand witnesses. You lie in the gate for a month. The sedan chair goes past once, slowly. You look at the curtain until it twitches shut.

choices.text: Take to the hills for a season

effects.log: A season in the hills on the bitter leaf. The crew goes home. The horn is cleaner for it.

choices.text: Walk straight at the sedan chair

ok.log: The bearers drop the chair and run. Inside, a fat official in a nightcap, who decides at once that horn powder is a superstition. The crew goes with him.

fail.log: The nets come from both sides. You get through, but slowly. (-14 health)

events.text: An alchemist, {npc}, in a stained robe that smells of mercury, sits down across from you under the drum tower and speaks to you as an equal, which is rare. "I will be honest, since I gather I must be. I want your horn. Not to kill you: a shaving. A powder that lets the drinker see lies would end a great deal of evil. Is that not what you want too?"

choices.text: "A shaving of my horn would make the drinker see enemies everywhere. No."

effects.log: {npc} is quiet for a while. "You know that?" {he} asks. You do not know it. The horn knows it. {npc} goes away to think, which is more than most do.

choices.text: Lower your head at {npc} (the horn: a lie)

effects.log: {npc} was honest about the shaving, and lying about the buyer: a sect that wants the powder for its interrogation hall. When the horn comes down, {npc} gets up and bows, ruefully. "Worth trying," {he} says. You suppose it was.

choices.text: Let {him} take one shaving, to see what comes of it

effects.log: A shaving like a fingernail. Your horn aches for a month. Years later you hear of an alchemist in the south who trusts nobody, not even {his} own hands, and grinds {his} own rice. (-6 Clarity)

events.text: The petition drum hangs on the gate tower above the place where you sleep: a great barrel of red-lacquered wood and ox-hide, with a pair of sticks on a peg. Anyone wronged, the law says, may beat it, and the king must hear. In practice there is a guard, {npc}, who stands under it all day and turns away anyone in rags, anyone from the provinces, anyone who has not been to the magistrate and the governor and the inspector-general first.
events.arc: The Drum on the Gate Tower

choices.text: Lie down between the guard and the steps up to the drum

effects.log: Nobody turns anyone away past a horned beast. The drum sounds three times that month instead of once a year. The guard stops trying to stand in front of the steps and starts standing beside you.

choices.text: Watch who {npc} turns away, and who {he} lets by

effects.log: The ragged and the provincial, turned away, mostly fairly by the rules. And now and then, someone well dressed who is turned away very fast, and someone who slips {npc} a coin and is let up. You remember the faces.

choices.text: Lie down under the drum and sleep

effects.log: It is the quietest place in the capital, under a drum nobody is allowed to beat. You sleep like a stone.

events.text: You can speak now, and the first human you speak to is {npc}, the guard of the drum, at midnight, when the square is empty. {He} nearly drops the spear. Then {he} asks, because people always do, whether you are really what they say. You ask {him} instead why {he} turned away the farmer this morning, the one with the deed.
events.arc: The Drum on the Gate Tower

choices.text: "The farmer's case was against a minister's steward. Who pays you?"

effects.log: {npc} tells it all in a rush, as people do when the horn is on them: the minister's steward, a string of cash every month, petitions about the steward's land turned away before they reach the drum. "I have a family," {npc} says. You say that the farmer does too. The next morning the farmer is let up the steps.

choices.text: "Why?" and nothing else. Let {him} answer

ok.log: "Because I was paid to," {npc} says at last, as if the words had been waiting. "By a steward. Every month." {He} looks at the drum. "I would like to be paid by nobody. How does a person do that?" You say: start tomorrow. {He} does.

fail.log: {npc} says the farmer had not been to the governor first, which is true, and that the rules are the rules, which is also true. Every sentence is true. The whole of it is a lie. You cannot catch hold of it.

choices.text: "You stand under a drum for the wronged. What does that make you?"

effects.log: {npc} does not answer. But the next week {he} lets up a woman in rags from the far south, and stands behind the petitioner while the drum is beaten, very straight, as if {he} had been waiting years for someone to ask.

events.text: Midnight, and the drum sounds: not with the sticks. With bare hands. A slave, {npc}, thin as a rake, branded on the wrist, is beating the ox-hide with both fists and has been for some time, because the knuckles are bleeding. The guards are running up. A slave who beats the drum is flogged, the guards say, for the impudence, whatever the case.
events.arc: The Drum on the Gate Tower

choices.text: Stand up between the guards and the drum, and speak

mem.note: stood for me at the drum

effects.log: "Let it be heard," you say, and every guard stops. The case comes out in the morning: a master who sold a slave's children after promising them freedom on a deathbed, and an heir who burned the will. The horn is warm on every word. The case is heard. The will is found, half burned, in the heir's own chest.

choices.text: Lie down at the slave's feet, so the guards must step over you

effects.log: No guard will step over you. They stand on the steps and argue, and while they argue the palace wakes, and a secretary is sent down to see what the noise is. The case is heard because it is too late not to hear it.

choices.text: Ask {npc} first, quietly, whether every word will be true

effects.log: {npc} looks at you with eyes like two wells. "Every word," {he} says. The horn agrees. You stand up and let the guards see your horn, and they decide that the flogging can wait.

events.text: The king does not come down to the drum. The king sends a royal secretary, {npc}, a smooth person in green silk with a writing case, who hears the petitions in a small room by the gate and writes them down for the throne. You lie in the doorway. You notice that the brush stops moving whenever a petition names certain families.
events.arc: The Drum on the Gate Tower

choices.text: Lower your head at the brush whenever it stops (the horn: a lie)

effects.log: Every time the brush stops, your horn comes down onto the writing table, very gently, beside it. After the third time {npc} starts to write again, everything, with a face like a shut box. That record reaches the king. It also reaches certain families.

choices.text: Ask the petitioners to say their cases again, louder, at the gate

effects.log: You cannot make a secretary write. You can make the square hear. A petition repeated at the gate to a hundred listeners is hard to lose between a room and a throne.

choices.text: Go to the throne yourself and lie down in the hall

ok.log: The hall is full of ministers who all stop talking. The king, young and tired, looks at the horned beast lying in the middle of the floor, and asks what it wants. You tell the throne: its drum is heard by a brush that stops. The king sends for the brush.

fail.log: The guards turn you back at the second gate with spears, very politely. By evening {npc} knows exactly who tried to go over {his} head.

events.text: The drum sounds on the gate tower, and you go down to hear who beat it. Today it is {npc}, from a province you have never seen, with a petition written on mulberry paper by a village scribe and a story about a stolen field.
events.arc: The Drum on the Gate Tower

choices.text: Listen, and let the horn decide

ok.log: The horn is warm. Every word of it is true. You stand beside {npc} when the secretary comes down, and the petition goes up to the throne with a beast's weight behind it.

fail.log: The horn is silent. You lie down and do not lower your head at anyone. The petition goes up on its own merits, which is how it should go, perhaps.

choices.text: The horn is clean today: say plainly whether it is true (the horn: true)

effects.log: True from the first line to the seal. You say so before the secretary, before the guards, before the square. The field is returned by the next spring.

choices.text: Ask {npc} who wrote the petition, and who paid for it

effects.log: A village scribe; three households paid together, in eggs. {npc} has walked forty days. It is not proof. It is not nothing. You walk with {him} to the secretary's door.

events.text: Years under the drum. You have learned what it is for. It is not for the cases the magistrate could hear. It is for the ones nobody else will: the last door, after the magistrate and the governor and the inspector-general have all shut theirs. And so every person who beats it has been refused three times, and is either very wronged, or very determined to be believed.
events.arc: The Drum on the Gate Tower

choices.text: The more doors shut, the more carefully you must listen

effects.log: Three refusals make an honest person desperate and a liar polished. You learn to listen for the polish. It is the hardest thing the horn has ever done.

choices.text: The drum should not need you. Make the other doors open

effects.log: You start going to the inspector-general's gate in the mornings and lying there, so the petitioners see that door before they need the last one. Fewer reach the drum. More are heard.

events.text: A son, {npc}, beats the drum in mourning clothes, sobbing: {his} father's second wife poisoned {his} father's soup, and will poison {him} next, and take the house. The whole square is moved. The stepmother is brought before the gate with hands tied, very pale and very calm. By the old law of the realm, if the accusation is false, the accuser takes the punishment sought for the accused. {He} has asked for the stepmother's death.

choices.text: Lower your head at the son (the horn: a lie)

effects.log: Every tear is real and every word is false. The horn finds the lie under the grief, the way a tongue finds a stone in rice: the father died of a failing heart, and the son wants the house. You lower your head at {him} before the whole square. The stepmother's hands are untied. By the old law, {he} will suffer what {he} sought for the stepmother.

choices.text: Lie down between them, and ask for the physician who saw the body

effects.log: The square waits for the beast to point, and the beast asks for a physician instead. It takes a month. In the end, the physician says heart, not poison. You did not point, and you were not wrong, and the case is not yet closed.

choices.text: Look at both of them, a long time, before you choose

ok.log: The stepmother's calm is the calm of somebody who has already wept everything. The son's grief is real, but it is grief at the wrong thing: at a house that is not yet {his}. You lower your head at {npc}, and the square gasps.

fail.log: The son's tears move you. You lower your head at the stepmother. Months later, at the trial, a physician proves the father died of a failing heart, and the son is sentenced for false accusation, and the stepmother never looks at you again. Something in your horn cracks, very quietly. (A crack: -8 Clarity)

events.text: Before the trial you find the son, {npc}, alone in the gate-house where the accusers wait, and you speak to {him}. By the old law, if {he} is found false {he} will be put to death, as {he} asked for the stepmother. There is still time to withdraw the accusation and take a flogging for a hasty word instead.

choices.text: "Withdraw it now, and live"

ok.log: {npc} looks at you for a long time. Then {he} goes to the officials and withdraws it, shaking, and takes forty strokes and a fine of half the house. It is a lie unmasked, and a life spared. The stepmother keeps the other half.

fail.log: "You are a beast," {npc} says. "What do you know of fathers and houses?" {He} holds to it. The trial goes on.

choices.text: "I know. So will they." And nothing more

effects.log: You only say that, and go. In the morning {npc} is found in the gate-house, writing a confession. The old law takes its course. You lie in the square through the whole of it.

choices.text: Say nothing. It is {his} choice to make

effects.log: You look at {npc} and go. Some truths should not be told to a person. They have to arrive.

events.text: An old man comes to the gate on two sticks: the accuser's grandfather, the dead man's father. He sits down in front of you and does not beg, which is worse. "He is the last of my blood," he says. "If he dies by the old law, my line ends. The woman is free; nobody is hurt now. Can a haechi not lower its horn, once, for an old man?"

choices.text: Lower the horn for the old man: speak for mercy at the trial

effects.log: You ask the court to spare the grandson his life. The court, which has never heard a haechi ask for anything, takes the ask as an order and sentences him to exile instead. The old man dies that winter knowing his line goes on, somewhere in the far north. (-3 Clarity)

choices.text: "The law that would have killed her will judge him. I only see."

effects.log: He nods, slowly, as if he had known. "Then see," he says. "And remember that I asked." You remember. You always will.

choices.text: Ask the stepmother what she wants

effects.log: She is a long time answering. "I want him gone from the house," she says at last. "I do not want him dead. I have had enough of death in that house." The court hears her. He is exiled. The old man bows to her, at the gate, for a long time.

events.text: The stepmother, {npc}, comes to the drum tower a year later, alone, with a basket of chinaberry leaves {he} picked {him}self on the south slope. "You were the only one who looked at me as if I might be telling the truth," {npc} says. "Everyone else had decided by my face."

choices.text: "Your face was calm. Calm is not guilt."

mem.note: believed me

effects.log: {npc} laughs, unexpectedly, and sits down and feeds you leaves one by one. {He} comes every spring after that with a basket, until {he} is too old to carry it, and then {he} sends a grandchild who is not of {his} blood but who calls {him} grandmother anyway.

choices.text: "I only looked. The horn did the rest."

effects.log: "Then thank your horn for me," {npc} says, and puts the basket down, and goes. The leaves are the bitterest you have had in the capital.

events.text: A great swordsman, {npc}, famous in three provinces, beats the drum against a rival school's master: murder, by poison needle, at a tournament. The square fills with martial men. Your horn goes cold at {npc}. And {npc}, who has heard of you, has come with forty disciples, and stares at you over their heads as if daring you to point.

choices.text: Point. A lie does not grow true because it has forty swords

mem.note: pointed at me before the whole capital

effects.log: You lower your head at the greatest swordsman in three provinces, and forty swords come half out of their sheaths in the square. The king's guard comes down the steps. {npc} will not accept the old law; {he} walks out of the capital with {his} school around {him}, an outlaw by sunset. Three provinces know why.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to repeat the accusation, slowly, word by word, before the court

ok.log: Slowly, word by word, a lie gets heavier. Halfway through {npc} changes the hour of the tournament, and the court notices, and the case falls apart in {his} hands like wet paper.

fail.log: {npc} tells it slowly and perfectly, a polished stone of a lie. The court is impressed. You are not, but you cannot prove it, and the rival master is held for trial.

choices.text: Lie down. Forty swords in a crowded square is a slaughter waiting
