effects.log: You lower the horn so the square does not run red. The case goes to the court, slowly, where it takes six years and nobody dies of it, and the rival master is freed for want of proof. The lie is never named. (-3 Clarity)

events.text: You understand it at last, lying under the drum. The horn's natural prey is not the thief or the brawler, who lie to save themselves. It is the one who lies in the name of justice: who beats the drum with real tears and false words, and asks for someone else's death. That lie wears the face of the very thing you are for.

choices.text: Hunt it above all others

effects.log: From then on, when a petitioner weeps at the drum, you listen hardest to the tears. Most are true. The ones that are not, you never forget.

choices.text: Pity it, a little. It is often grief gone wrong

effects.log: The son wanted a house because he had lost a father. The swordsman wanted a rival dead because he had lost a fight. You still point. But you point more slowly now, and you lie down beside them afterwards.

events.text: The king rides out to the royal tombs, and the road is lined with people on their knees. A servant, {npc}, gets up from among them, runs into the road before the palanquin, and strikes a little brass gong, again and again: {his} dead husband's field was taken by a magistrate's cousin, and nobody will hear {him}. The officials say {he} is mad. The guards step forward.

choices.text: Walk out into the road and lie down beside {npc} (the horn: true)

mem.note: lay down beside me in the road

effects.log: {He} is not mad; every word is true. The procession stops because a horned beast is lying in the road with its ears laid back beside a servant with a gong. The palanquin curtain moves. A hand beckons. The case is heard by the roadside, on a mat, there and then.

choices.text: Walk out and stand between the guards and {npc}

effects.log: The guards will not go through you. The procession stops. An official runs up, sweating, to ask what the beast wants. You cannot say yet what is true: the horn has not decided. But the gong has been heard, and that is what a gong is for.

choices.text: Stay on the verge and listen first

ok.log: Every strike of the gong and every word between: true. You get up off the verge before the guards reach {npc}, and they stop when you do.

fail.log: The noise, the banners, the shouting: the horn cannot find the thread. By the time it does, {npc} has been dragged off the road. The procession goes on.

events.text: The official in charge of the gong petitions, {npc}, comes to the drum tower with a smile and a file. "The servant is unwell in the mind," {he} says to you. "The dead husband sold that field before dying. Here is the deed." The deed is very fine, on good paper, with a red seal.

choices.text: Lower your head at the deed (the horn: a lie)

effects.log: The paper is new, the seal is borrowed, and the horn is ice. You lower it onto the deed in {npc}'s hands. {npc} stops smiling. The magistrate's cousin is summoned, the old village scribe is found, and the field goes back to the servant before the rains.

choices.text: Ask to see the village where the field is

effects.log: You walk four days to the village and lie down at the field. The neighbours tell you everything, once they see you: the cousin, the night the boundary stones moved, the scribe who was paid. You walk back with the truth in your horn and the whole village behind you.

choices.text: Accept the deed: it looks very fine

effects.log: You nod at the deed. The servant is sent home to the provinces with a warning, and the field stays with the cousin. The servant was right. You were looking at the seal. Something in your horn cracks, very quietly. (A crack: -8 Clarity)

events.text: {npc} is back at the drum tower, with a rice cake wrapped in a cloth. {He} has {his} field again. {He} has walked twenty days to say so. "They told me in the village I was mad for going," {he} says. "I told them a horned beast lay down beside me in front of the king. Now they think I am really mad."

choices.text: "Tell them again. One of them will believe you"

effects.log: {npc} laughs. "One already does," {he} says. "My daughter. The child wants to be a haechi when grown." {He} leaves the rice cake. You eat it, though it is sweet, because some sweet things do not cloud the horn.

choices.text: Lay your ears back, and bow to {him}

effects.log: The guards at the tower see the beast bow to a servant in a patched coat, and tell it in the barracks, and the barracks tell it in the taverns, and by winter the gong-strikers on the royal road are treated a little more gently.

events.text: The king rides out again, and this time the road is lined with gongs: a hundred poor people, each with a gong or a pot lid or a kitchen knife and a bowl, waiting to strike. The officials are frantic. Someone has told them all that a horned beast will lie down beside them.

choices.text: Walk the whole length of the road, and lie down beside each true one

effects.log: All day, in the dust, down the road. Down beside the woman with the pot lid. Past the man with the knife and bowl, who is lying. Down beside the old man with the gong. By evening sixty petitions have been heard and the king, who rode out to visit his ancestors, rides home very thoughtful. (-5 health)

choices.text: Stay at the drum: if every petition comes to the road, the drum dies

effects.log: You stay under the drum. Some of the hundred, disappointed, come to the drum instead, which has a guard who now lets them up the steps. The road is for those the drum cannot reach.

events.text: The Office of the Inspector-General sends for you: a young inspector, {npc}, in the black hat of the censors, with a beast like you embroidered on the front of it, ears laid back. The censors meet every day at a fixed hour in their tea hall, drink one cup together in silence, and only then speak of who in the realm is lying. "We would like you to drink tea with us," {npc} says, and then, embarrassed, "or at least to lie in the hall while we do."

choices.text: Go and lie in the tea hall

mem.note: came to our tea

effects.log: A long low hall, mats, a celadon bottle, nine censors and one cup each. The tea is bitter: they know. Nobody speaks until the cups are empty. Then they speak of ministers as plainly as farmers speak of rain, and look at you after every name.

choices.text: Ask why they drink tea before judging

effects.log: "So we do not judge hot," {npc} says. "The cup cools the hand. A judgement made in anger is a lie told to yourself." You go to the hall. It is the first human rule you have heard that a haechi could have made.

choices.text: Lie down outside instead. A hall is a kind of leash

effects.log: You lie on the steps outside the tea hall. The censors find this entirely proper, and leave the door open, and talk loud enough for you to hear.

events.text: Your first night tea. Seven censors meet after dark near the house of an official accused of selling the relief grain meant for a starving province. They sit on mats in the lane before the gate and drink tea by lantern. A white board is propped against the wall, a bundle of thorn branches already cut. One by one, {npc} reads the crimes, and after each one, all seven look at you.

choices.text: Hold your horn level at every true line, and lower it at none of the false (the horn: true)

effects.log: Six lines true, the horn says. Two not: rumours, spite. The censors brush out the two and write the six on the white board. It goes up over the gate. The thorn branches go across it, and seven names are signed underneath. In the morning the street reads the board, and nobody is surprised.

choices.text: Get up and walk away before the board goes up: the horn is not sure

effects.log: The censors are angry. The tea goes cold. But nobody hangs a board without the beast, now that the beast is here, and the case goes back to be examined for another season. It is not cowardice. It is the tea, cooling the hand.

choices.text: Listen to every line, and judge as best you can

ok.log: Line by line, slowly, the horn warms and cools. By the end you are sure. You lower your head at the gate. The board goes up and the thorns go across.

fail.log: The tea is too strong and the lanterns too dim. You nod at all eight lines. Two of them were false: the official sold grain, but never beat the tenants; a cousin did, and the cousin's crime is written on the official's board. Something in your horn cracks, very quietly. (A crack: -8 Clarity)

events.text: After the board goes up, the censors go home. {npc} stays, sitting on the mat in the dark lane with a cold cup, looking at the thorn branches across the gate. "Can I ask you something?" {he} says. "Are we right? Not about the official. About this. Thorns and a board in the night. It feels like a curse."

choices.text: "It is a curse. On the truth's side, this time. Keep asking that question"

effects.log: {npc} laughs, quietly, the way people do when they have been answered and not comforted. "I will," {he} says. You think {he} will. It is why you will trust {his} boards.

choices.text: "Ask the people in the house"

effects.log: In the morning {npc} goes back and talks to the official's servants and children through the thorns. It changes nothing about the board. It changes something about {npc}.

events.text: Morning before the thorn-sealed gate. The servants of the house are climbing out over the side wall with bundles, one by one. A small child, {npc}, is sitting on the step inside the thorns, holding a doll, waiting for somebody to come back for {him}. The board above says everything the father did. It says nothing about the child.

choices.text: Push aside one thorn branch, carefully, and let the child out

effects.log: The thorns tear your muzzle. You make a gap a child can fit through, and {npc} comes out holding the doll, and takes hold of your mane, and you walk {him} to the inspector's house, because you can think of nowhere else. (-3 health)

choices.text: Lie down outside the thorns until a relative comes

effects.log: All day you lie outside the thorns and the child lies inside, looking at you through the branches. At dusk an aunt comes from the country with a handcart. The child waves to you from the cart. You did not cause the board. You helped hang it.

events.text: A second night tea, and a different lane. This time the accuser is a senior censor, {npc}, who has prepared the board {him}self, very neatly, every crime in fine characters. The accused is a minister of the other faction. {npc} hands you the first cup of tea, which nobody has ever done, and smiles.

choices.text: Lower your head at {npc}'s neat board (the horn: a lie)

effects.log: Every crime on the board is invented, in fine characters. The accused minister is greedy and dull and innocent of all of it. You lower your head at the board, and then at {npc}, and the other censors put their cups down very carefully. It is not the minister's gate that gets thorns this year.

choices.text: Refuse the cup. Refuse the board. Walk away

effects.log: You get up and leave the lane, and the other censors, after a long moment, get up and leave it too. {npc} is left alone with a neat board and nobody to sign it.

choices.text: Drink the tea, and judge as you can

ok.log: The tea is sweet. Tea at the night tea is never sweet. That is enough to make you look again, and the second look finds it: the board is a lie. You knock it face down in the dust.

fail.log: The tea is sweet and your horn is slow. You nod at the board. The minister is cast out, and dies in the country two winters later, still swearing innocence. The minister was innocent. Something in your horn cracks, very quietly. (A crack: -11 Clarity)

events.text: You have sat many night teas now. The tea at the start, bitter and cooling; the board; the thorns; the names. A house cast out by a board in the night is never quite let back in, even when the board is right. And you have learned that the tea is not to cool the censors' hands. It is to give them time to be afraid of being wrong.

choices.text: Be afraid of being wrong, every time. It is the price of the board

effects.log: You never sit a night tea again without a moment, before the first line is read, of plain cold fear. The censors notice. They start to wait for it before they lift their cups.

choices.text: A board that is right is a mercy to the street

effects.log: A street that knows who robbed it can stop being robbed. You sit the night tea with a heavier certainty after that, and the lanes of the capital are a little more honest, and a little more frightened.

events.text: The censors' hat-maker, {npc}, sets up a stool in front of you with a frame of black horsehair and a box of coloured threads. For three generations the censors have worn a beast like you on their hats. Nobody, {npc} admits, has ever actually seen one. "Hold still," {he} says. "Ears down, if you would."

choices.text: Lay your ears flat and hold still all day

effects.log: The new hats come out right: a single horn, scales like frost, ears laid flat. The censors put them on and are unusually quiet that week. A sliver of your sight goes with each stitch. You feel it go, like a thread drawn out of a sleeve. (-1 Clarity)

choices.text: Shake your head so the horn rings, so the stitcher hears it

effects.log: {npc} stops with the needle in the air. "That," {he} says. "Can I put that in?" You do not know if a sound can be embroidered. {npc} tries, with silver thread round the horn. The hats are said to ring faintly when a liar speaks to the wearer. It is probably not true.

choices.text: Get up and walk out. Your face is not for hats

effects.log: {npc} draws you from memory anyway, from your back going out of the door. The hats that year have a beast with a very good tail and no face at all.

events.text: At the royal lecture, where the king reads the classics with the scholars at dawn, a young censor, {npc}, comes without the hat. The hall goes cold. Not wearing the hat before the throne is an insult to the office, and the senior censors are already writing the reprimand. {npc} stands bareheaded and does not explain.

choices.text: Walk into the hall and lie down beside the bareheaded censor

effects.log: The beast whose face is on the hat lies down beside the one who would not wear it. The hall does not know what to make of it. The reprimand is written, but it is not sent. Afterwards {npc} will not look at you.

choices.text: Lower your head at {npc}: something is being hidden (the horn: a lie)

effects.log: The horn says {npc} is hiding something, and {npc} knows the horn says so. {He} goes white and stays white through the whole of the lecture. The reprimand goes in. {He} is put to copying records at the back of the office, and still does not explain.

choices.text: Stay outside. A hat is the censors' business

effects.log: You hear about it at the gate: a reprimand, a dismissal coming. You remember the face. Somebody who will not wear your face has a reason.

events.text: {npc}, the young censor who would not wear the hat, finds you under the drum tower at night. "I could not put your face on," {he} says. "Not that week. I told a lie on Tuesday: to my mother, about where I had been. It was nothing. But I could not wear you over it. They say the hat sees."

choices.text: "Tell the truth at home, and put the hat back on"

mem.note: told me to wear the hat again

effects.log: {npc} goes home and tells the mother, who laughs and cuffs {him}, and the next morning {he} goes to the office with the hat on and asks to be reprimanded properly, for the right reason. The senior censors have never had such a request. They keep {him} on.

choices.text: "The hat is thread. You saw your own lie without it. Keep that"

effects.log: {npc} is quiet for a long time. "Then I will wear it," {he} says, "to remind me I do not need it." It is the best reason anyone has ever given you for wearing your face.

choices.text: Lower the horn: a small lie to a mother is not the office's affair

effects.log: You say nothing about it. {npc} is dismissed, as the office decides. {He} goes home to a mother who never knows why. (-3 Clarity)

events.text: Years later, an inspector in the censors' hat comes up the street to the drum tower, grey at the temples, and you know the walk: {npc}, who would not wear your face. {He} wears it now, every day, and is said to be the only censor in the office whom both factions are afraid of.

choices.text: Lay your ears back to {him}, as to the upright

effects.log: {npc} stops in the street and bows to you, hat and all. The street sees a beast and a censor bowing to each other, and nobody is quite sure who is honouring whom. Both, probably.

choices.text: Shake your head so your horn rings, and listen for the hat to answer

effects.log: Silver thread cannot ring. But {npc} touches the hat as if something had moved in it, and laughs, and walks on lighter.

events.text: The new Inspector-General is to wear you on the chest: a square of silk sewn on the front of the robe, a beast with one horn among clouds and waves. The embroiderer, {npc}, an old person with eyes like a hawk's, counts your scales twice, then a third time, and asks you very politely to lay your ears back and keep them there until spring.

choices.text: Keep your ears back all winter

effects.log: A whole winter with your ears flat. When the badge is finished, the scales are right, every one, and the eyes are right, and the horn is a single line of white silk that seems to have light in it. A sliver of your sight goes with it. (-1 Clarity)

choices.text: Let {npc} count, but not take the eyes

effects.log: {npc} stitches the eyes shut, as if sleeping. "A badge that does not see," {he} says, "cannot see wrongly." It is the most popular badge the office ever has. Nobody is afraid of it.

events.text: The Inspector-General wears the badge to the council for the first time. You lie on the steps outside. Halfway through the morning he comes out alone, sits down beside you, and is quiet for a while. "A minister told me a lie just now," he says. "A small one, about a canal. I have been in this office twenty years and I never saw one before. I always knew afterwards. I never saw it at the time."

choices.text: Lay your ears back. A sliver of you is doing its work

effects.log: He nods slowly. Then he goes back in and asks the minister about the canal again, and the minister, who has never been asked twice, tells him the truth by mistake.

choices.text: Shake your head. Sight that comes from a badge goes with the badge

effects.log: "Then I must learn to see without it," he says, "before I retire." He starts coming to the tea hall early, to sit beside you in silence. In his last years he can tell a lie without the badge, a little, sometimes.

events.text: {npc}, the embroiderer, very old now, comes to you with a square of silk and an unfinished beast on it. "For my grandchild," {he} says. "Who passed the examination this spring and goes to a county court in the south, where they will try to buy every judgement. One more sliver. A small one. You have so many."

choices.text: Lay your ears back for the last stitches

effects.log: The badge goes south on the grandchild's chest. Years later, a southern county is said to have a judge nobody can buy, who looks at bribes as if they were on fire. (-1 Clarity)

choices.text: "I have fewer than you think." Refuse, gently

effects.log: {npc} nods and finishes the beast from memory instead. "Then my grandchild will have to see with their own eyes," {he} says. "Perhaps that is better." You think it is. You also think you should have given it.

events.text: The court has split like a log: the faction of the Old Pines, whose leaders live east of the palace, and the faction of the Young Bamboo, whose leaders live west. Each sends you a scroll. The Pines' scroll lists the lies of the Bamboo, and every one of them is true. The Bamboo's scroll lists the lies of the Pines, and every one of those is true as well.

choices.text: Butt the lies on both scrolls, one by one, before the whole court

effects.log: You go through both scrolls in the council hall, lowering your head at Pines and Bamboo alike, all morning. By noon both factions hate you equally, which the old men of the court say has never happened to anybody, and is perhaps the best thing that can happen to a judge.

choices.text: Lie down between the two scrolls and look at neither

effects.log: Both factions read this as you favouring the other one. Both are wrong. You lie there a week, and the court learns that the horn does not point at a list. It points at a person, standing in front of it.

choices.text: Take the Pines' scroll and butt only the Bamboo

effects.log: Every butt is true. The Bamboo fall from office one by one. The Pines are delighted and send you leaves every week. The horn knows exactly what it has been made into: a true thing, held by one hand. (-6 Clarity)

events.text: A leader of the Old Pines, {npc}, a great scholar with a soft voice, comes to the tea hall after the others have gone and sits down in front of you. "I will not offer you silver," {he} says. "I offer you a purpose. The Bamboo will ruin the realm. Point at them when I bring them to you, and only then, and the realm will be clean in ten years. A horn needs a hand to guide it."

choices.text: "A horn that is guided is a spear. No."

mem.note: would not take my hand

effects.log: {npc} bows, without anger. "Then you will be used by whoever is cleverest," {he} says, "instead of by me." It is not a threat. It is worse. It is a prediction.

choices.text: Lower your head at {npc}: the purpose is a lie (the horn: a lie)

effects.log: The soft voice believes every word about the realm, and is lying about one thing: the ten years. {npc} means to rule for forty. When the horn comes down {he} smiles, almost with relief. "Good," {he} says. "Then you are not for sale even in the coin I value most."

choices.text: Accept, for the realm's sake

effects.log: You say yes. From then on {npc} brings you people, and you lower your head at them, and every butt is true, and every one of them is Bamboo. It is a bribe paid in purpose instead of silver. The horn knows the difference is very small. (-8 Clarity)

events.text: The Bamboo bring twelve Pines officials to the courtyard at once and ask you to look at each. You do. Eight of them are lying about something: a gift, a nephew's post, a field. All small. If you lower your head at eight, the king will have a reason to purge the whole faction, and the scholars who serve it, and the scholars' students.

choices.text: Point at all eight. The truth is the truth

effects.log: Eight butts. Eight small lies. The purge that follows takes eighty men, few of whom told any lie at all. You were right eight times, and somewhere in the provinces seventy-two families are packing for exile. The horn is clean, and it does not feel clean.

choices.text: Lower the horn for all twelve, this once

effects.log: You lie down and look at the sky. Twelve men go home. The Bamboo are furious; the Pines are puzzled. The purge does not come. The eight small lies stay where they were, heavy, under the roofs of eight houses. (-4 Clarity)

choices.text: Point only at the one whose lie hurt someone

ok.log: One of the eight took a widow's field. You point at him, and only him. The Bamboo complain that the beast is soft. The king, who does not want a purge either, is quietly grateful.

fail.log: You try to weigh eight lies against each other while two factions watch, and the horn gets tangled in the weighing. You point at nobody, and both sides call it cowardice.

events.text: A faction you shamed does not forget. Three nights running, someone has left a dead crow on the drum tower steps. On the fourth, men with nets and hooded lanterns come to the tower at the hour when the guards change.

choices.text: Ring the drum yourself, with your head

effects.log: Boom. The whole palace wakes. The men with nets find themselves surrounded by guards, servants and a half-dressed royal secretary, and decide they were never there. The crows stop.

choices.text: Fight them on the steps

ok.log: Four men, four nets, and you go through all of them. In the morning the guards find the nets on the steps and a hooded lantern with a minister's crest scratched off.

fail.log: A net, a hook, a blow to the head. You wake in a cart outside the walls and break out of it before the city gate. (-25 health)
fail.deathCause: faction hirelings with nets on the drum tower steps

choices.text: Go to the censors' tea hall and lie there until it blows over

effects.log: The censors take it as a great compliment. Nobody sends hirelings into the Office of the Inspector-General. The crows stop, eventually.

events.text: You lie on the steps of the council hall and listen to the two factions through the paper doors. Each is right about the other. Each, if it wins, will do what the other did. You understand now what the horn is in a court: not a judge. A weapon, lying on the floor, waiting for whichever hand picks it up first.

choices.text: Then never lie still where a hand can reach. Move

effects.log: You start sleeping somewhere different every night: the drum tower, the tea hall, the market, the south slope with the chinaberry trees. A weapon that will not stay put is hard to pick up.

choices.text: Then pick yourself up, before anyone else does

effects.log: You choose your own cases from now on: you walk into the council when you choose, and point at whom you choose, Pines and Bamboo alike. The court is terrified of you. It is a little better than being a spear.

events.text: A righteous sect in the mountains sends three disciples down to fetch you, very respectfully: a manual has gone from the scripture pavilion, and the sect would like the matter judged by something that cannot be argued with. In the discipline hall two disciples kneel: the elder's own son, {npc}, in fine white silk, and a thin outer disciple who sweeps the yards. The elder's son found the manual in the sweeper's bedding.

choices.text: Lower your head at the elder's son (the horn: a lie)

effects.log: {npc} put it there. The horn knew it before {he} finished bowing. You lower your head at the fine silk, and the hall goes so quiet you can hear the pines outside. The elder looks at {his} son for a long time, and then at you, and you are not sure which of you will be forgiven first.

choices.text: Lie down at the doors: you judge lies, not sects

effects.log: The sect is offended. The sweeper is not expelled, for lack of a verdict, and works the yards with your shadow at the gate for a month. The manual turns up in the scripture pavilion again, very quietly, one morning.

choices.text: Walk round both, slowly, and judge as you can

ok.log: The sweeper smells of straw and terror. {npc} smells of the scripture pavilion's incense, deep in the sleeves, where it should not be. You lower your head at the silk.

fail.log: The sweeper will not look up, and you take that for guilt. It was only fear. The sweeper is expelled down the mountain, and {npc} watches you go with a very small smile. Something in your horn cracks, very quietly. (A crack: -8 Clarity)

events.text: The sect's master comes down the mountain to you in person: a tall grave old person in white, a great name in the murim. "The sect's honour is a thousand disciples' honour," the master says. "I know what my elder's son did. It will be dealt with, inside the walls. Say nothing outside them. In return, the sect's own spring, above the falls, the cleanest water in three provinces, is yours for a quiet year."

choices.text: Refuse, and go on saying nothing anyway: it is the sect's to deal with

effects.log: The master looks at you for a long time, understanding that the silence is free and therefore cannot be bought back. The son is sent to a far branch temple to cook rice for years. It is dealt with.

choices.text: Refuse, and tell the murim at the next market town

effects.log: A beast lying in the market square with its horn lowered at a sect banner. The murim talks of nothing else for a season. The sect's honour is dented; the sweeper is a hero in the taverns. The master never forgives you, and is never quite wrong about anything again.

choices.text: Accept the spring for a quiet year

effects.log: It is the cleanest water you have ever tasted, and every morning when you drink it, the horn remembers what it cost. A clean spring bought is not a clean spring. (-8 Clarity)

events.text: A wandering swordsman, {npc}, with a chipped sword and a good face, sits down across the stream from you and asks, without much hope, whether you can tell if a dead person lied. {His} master, on the deathbed, told {him} that the sect expelled them both for nothing. The sect says the master stole. {npc} has spent ten years not knowing which.

choices.text: Go with {npc} to the sect and look at the old record keeper

mem.note: showed me the truth about my master

ok.log: The record keeper swears the master stole, and the horn goes cold. Then {he} swears the master was expelled to make room for an elder's nephew, and the horn goes warm. {npc} sits down on the sect's steps and laughs and cries at once, for years.

fail.log: The record keeper is too old to lie well and too old to remember straight, and the horn gets nothing from either. {npc} thanks you anyway. "At least it is not that I did not ask," {he} says.

choices.text: Lie down and look at {npc}: the horn can only read the living

effects.log: You cannot read a dead master. You can read the one in front of you, who loved the master and is afraid of being a fool for it. You lay your ears back. {npc} understands it as "it is not foolish". It is the best you can do.

events.text: The sweeper from the discipline hall is a master now, with a small school of {his} own in the next valley. {npc} comes before you to take the oath of a new sect founder: to teach without favour, to judge {his} own disciples by the same law as strangers', and never to hide a disciple's crime for the school's honour. {He} wants you to hear it.

choices.text: Hear the oath, and remember it

effects.log: {npc} swears it, every line warm in the horn. Thirty years later you pass the school and lie at its gate, and the discipline hall inside judges a master's favourite exactly as it judges a sweeper. {npc} kept it.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to swear it again when {he} is old

effects.log: "An oath at the start is easy," {npc} agrees. Thirty years on, white-haired, {he} comes back down the valley to swear it again before you, and it is still warm, and {he} weeps a little with the relief of it.

events.text: In the deep pool under the cliff where the river leaves the capital, something long and dark lies coiled, and has lain there a hundred years, waiting. An Imugi: a great serpent that would be a dragon. It has heard about the beast with the horn. One evening it lifts its head out of the water and asks you, very politely, whether it is a dragon.

choices.text: Say only what is: "Not yet"

effects.log: The Imugi looks at you for a long time. "Not yet," it repeats, tasting the words. "Not no." It sinks back into the pool, and the water is very still. You are not sure whether you have been kind.

choices.text: Lower the horn. Some questions are not for a horn

effects.log: You lie down on the bank and say nothing. The Imugi waits a whole night for an answer, and then sinks, and you hear it, under the water, telling itself that the silence meant yes. (-3 Clarity)

choices.text: Ask it why it wants to know

effects.log: "Because if I am already a dragon," the Imugi says, "I can stop waiting." You understand then that it does not want the truth. It wants permission. A horn cannot give that.

events.text: The Imugi comes up out of the pool again, years later, and asks a different question. "I told a lie," it says. "To a fisherman, about a storm. I said I would bring it, and I did not, and he went out, and drowned. Does that make me less a dragon, or more a snake?"

choices.text: "It makes you one who lied. That is all the horn sees"

effects.log: The Imugi is quiet for a long time. "That is a smaller thing than I feared," it says, "and a heavier one." It goes down into the pool. In the spring the fisherman's widow finds a pearl on her step, and does not know why.

choices.text: "Go and tell the fisherman's family. Then ask me again"

effects.log: The Imugi goes down the river in the dark. You never learn what it said to the family, or in what shape. But the next time a storm comes up that river, it comes up gently, and every fisherman is home.

events.text: A storm in the night, of a kind the capital has never seen, and at dawn the deep pool under the cliff is empty. Far to the east, over the sea, a cloud stands up like a pillar with something long in it. Or it is only a cloud. On the bank, scratched in the mud by something that has no hands, there is one word.

choices.text: Look at the word until the horn says whether it is true

effects.log: The word is "Now". The horn is warm. Whatever went up out of that pool believed it, all the way up.

choices.text: Lie down on the bank and let the rain wash it out

effects.log: It was not written for you. You let the rain have it, and lie in the empty place where the serpent used to be, and the pool fills slowly with clear water.

events.text: A minister of the first rank invites you to a banquet in his pavilion over the lotus pond, which nobody refuses. The tables are low and endless: honey cakes, candied ginseng, persimmons in syrup, sweet rice liquor in celadon. The air is so sweet your horn goes soft at the edges. And among the guests there is one in pale silk, laughing behind a fan, whose shadow on the screen behind them is not quite the right shape.

choices.text: Eat nothing. Lie by the door with your mouth shut

effects.log: The minister is offended. The guests are amused. The guest in pale silk looks at you over the fan, once, with eyes the colour of honey, and smiles as if you had paid a compliment.

choices.text: Eat a little, to be polite

effects.log: One honey cake, one persimmon. By the end of the evening the guests' lies are all a pleasant blur, and you are fond of everyone. That is exactly what the cakes are for. (-4 Clarity)

choices.text: Watch the shadow on the screen

effects.log: When the lanterns move, the shadow has a tail. When they move again, it has more. You count nine before the guest, without turning round, moves the lantern.

events.text: The guest in pale silk sits down beside you at the banquet's edge with a plate of honey cakes and talks to you, pleasantly, about the minister. Every sentence the guest says is true. The minister is in debt. The minister's son is a fool. The minister's wife is cleverer than he is. And somewhere in the pattern of all those true things there is a lie the shape of the whole.

choices.text: Look for the lie in the shape, not the sentences (the horn: true)

effects.log: Every sentence is true, and every sentence makes you think the minister's wife is plotting. She is not. The guest is. The horn goes cold at the whole of it, at last, the way it goes cold at a fog. "Oh, well done," says the guest, delighted. "Nobody ever gets that."

choices.text: Lower your head at the guest

ok.log: You lower your horn at the pale silk. The guest laughs, a lovely sound, and does not move. "I have not told one lie," the guest says. "Not one." It is true. It is the truest lie you have ever met.

fail.log: Every sentence is warm in the horn, and you nod along, and by midnight you are sure the minister's wife is a traitor. In the morning you cannot remember why. (-3 Clarity)

choices.text: Eat the honey cakes the guest offers, one by one

effects.log: The guest feeds you cakes and truths, cakes and truths. The guest knows exactly what sweet things do to a horn. By the end of the night you would believe anything. Fortunately the guest is not, tonight, asking you to. (-6 Clarity)

events.text: In the garden behind the pavilion, by the lotus pond, the guest in pale silk finds you alone and drops the pleasantness like a fan. "Tell me, horned one," the guest says. "You see what is. So tell me what I am. I have worn so many faces I have forgotten which one is under the others."

choices.text: "You are the one asking. That is true"

effects.log: The guest is silent a long time. Then laughs, quietly, without any charm in it at all, which is the most honest sound you have heard all night. "That will do," the guest says. "For a hundred years or so."

choices.text: Lower the horn. That is not a lie, it is a wound

effects.log: You lie down by the pond and do not answer. The guest sits beside you until the lanterns burn out, and goes without a word. You think, perhaps, you did the kind thing. You are not sure the fox thinks so. (-3 Clarity)

choices.text: "A fox who has told no lie tonight, and done great harm"

effects.log: The guest's eyes go flat and gold. "Fair," says the Nine-Tailed Fox, quite pleasantly. "Do not come to any more banquets." In the morning the guest is gone, and the minister is ruined by the end of the year, by nothing anyone can name.

events.text: The minister of the lotus pavilion falls: debts, a fool son, a clever wife who leaves for her family's house in the south. None of it is a lie. None of it would have happened without a guest who has vanished. The court is baffled. The minister, at the gate on his way into exile, stops in front of you and asks whether you saw anything.

choices.text: "Everything you were told was true"

effects.log: He nods. It is not comfort. It is the truth, and he takes it with him into exile, where he writes a short book about honey cakes that nobody reads.

choices.text: Lower your head at the sweet things still on his cart

effects.log: He looks at the jars of syrup and boxes of cakes on the cart, and then, slowly, tips them into the ditch. "I never ate a bitter thing in my life," he says. "Perhaps I should start." He goes into exile with a bag of chinaberry leaves.

events.text: Years after the banquet a basket arrives at the drum tower with no sender: chinaberry leaves, the bitterest you have ever smelled, from a tree that grows only on the far southern islands. Under the leaves a single honey cake, and a strip of paper with one line in very elegant characters: For the next banquet.

choices.text: Eat the leaves, and leave the cake for the sparrows

effects.log: The leaves are so bitter your eyes water for a day. Your horn rings like ice for a month. The sparrows eat the cake and spend the afternoon telling each other lies with great conviction.

choices.text: Eat the cake too. A gift from an honest liar

effects.log: It is delicious, and the horn goes soft for a day, and you find you do not mind. Somewhere far to the south, you feel, someone is laughing. (-2 Clarity)

events.text: Another minister, another feast, another invitation that cannot be refused. The tables groan with sweet things, and every host has been told what sweetness does to a haechi's horn. They watch to see what you will eat.

choices.text: Bring your own chinaberry leaves and eat them at the gate

effects.log: The host is insulted. The guests are delighted. It becomes known in the capital that the haechi comes to feasts with its own lunch, and the hosts begin to put out a plate of bitter leaves by the gate, with a little embarrassment.

choices.text: Eat what is offered: refusing a minister has its own cost

effects.log: Candied ginseng, honey cakes, syrup. The host is pleased. Halfway through the evening he tells you a lie about his grain stores, and the horn only shrugs. (-3 Clarity)

choices.text: Do not go

effects.log: An empty place by the gate. The minister takes it badly, and somebody, later that month, mentions to some men with nets where you sleep.

events.text: At a feast, a minister of the treasury, {npc}, takes you aside to the garden and speaks of springs. {He} owns land in the hills with a spring as clear as the one you were born at. It could be yours, fenced, guarded, for ever. In exchange: one quiet year, while the treasury's accounts are examined by the censors.

choices.text: Lower your head at {npc} in the middle of the garden

effects.log: Fifty guests see the haechi lower its horn at the treasury minister among the peonies. The censors have their year's work handed to them. The minister has men with nets asking questions within the week.

choices.text: Tell {npc} the censors will be told nothing by you, and everything by the accounts

effects.log: "Then I am finished," {npc} says, quite calmly, and goes back to the feast, and drinks a great deal. The accounts do the rest. A haechi does not need to point at everything. Some things point at themselves.

choices.text: Take the spring

effects.log: The spring is beautiful and the year is quiet, and when the censors examine the treasury you are lying in the hills, washing in clear water that does not get your horn clean at all. (-8 Clarity)

events.text: The capital has a saying now: to bring a haechi a cake. It means to try to bribe somebody so honest it is embarrassing. Children say it to each other. A host, last month, served you a plate of chinaberry leaves arranged like a flower, and you ate it, and the whole court laughed, and you found that you did not mind.

choices.text: Let them laugh. A laughing court is not lying

effects.log: You eat the flower of leaves at every feast after that. Some hosts add a radish carved like a horn. It is the closest thing the capital has to affection for a beast that makes it uncomfortable, and you take it.

choices.text: Stop going to feasts at all

effects.log: The saying stays, and the plates of leaves are set out by gates you never come to, and slowly the joke turns into a custom nobody remembers the reason for.
